kernelIdea: Negation flips truth value. A statement and its negation are never both true and never both false.

kernels.l1: The opposite of a true telling is a not-true telling. They can't both be right at the same time.
kernels.l2: Every telling has an opposite. If the telling is true, its opposite is false. If the telling is false, its opposite is true. Never both.
kernels.l3: The negation of a statement flips its truth value: the negation of a true statement is false, and the negation of a false one is true.
kernels.l4: For a statement p, the negation ¬p is true exactly when p is false. p and ¬p are never both true and never both false.
kernels.l5: Negating a statement flips its truth value; ¬p is true iff p is false. In particular, ¬¬p has the same truth value as p.
kernels.l6: For any statement p, ¬p has truth value opposite to p's. Consequently p ∧ ¬p is always false (a contradiction) and p ∨ ¬p is always true (a tautology).
kernels.l7: Negation is the unary connective ¬ that inverts truth value; p and ¬p partition the truth-value assignments, and ¬¬p ≡ p.
kernels.l8: Negation is the involution on the Boolean algebra {T,F}: it satisfies ¬¬p = p, ¬(T)=F, and gives the law of excluded middle p ∨ ¬p and the law of non-contradiction ¬(p ∧ ¬p).
